metric.why: Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing. Fleet utilization is where the money hides in most enterprise estates, and it is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest.
metric.definition: The share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak.

reading.body:
Server utilization rate, the share of provisioned compute actually doing work over time, is the denominator that makes every data center efficiency claim true or false.

Most enterprise data centers carry substantial idle capacity. Servers provisioned but not running jobs burn power, depreciation, and license fees with zero output. This matters for AI because training and inference workloads are often bursty and unpredictable. A cluster sized for peak demand will sit partially idle most of the time. High utilization means either better job packing, faster hardware refresh cycles that match workload shifts, or willingness to turn off unused servers entirely. Low utilization means the cost per compute unit is genuinely higher than nameplate specs suggest, regardless of how efficient the hardware itself is.

This metric does not measure energy efficiency, thermal efficiency, or power per operation. It does not account for how quickly idle servers can be spun up again, which varies by workload type. It does not separate planned maintenance idle from demand-driven idle. It also does not tell you whether the constraint on utilization is architectural, economic, or regulatory.
